content.comment_body: Is it possible to achieve this? Another issue is that I get 2-10V instead of the full 0-10V range, even when using a resistor.

It is technically possible to connect a PC using a voltage divider directly to a 0-10V input, but this approach results in very imprecise measurements with low resolution. It is recommended to use a transmitter with a 0-10V output. For instance, see this example: [url]
What are your thoughts on this post? [url] Do you think it's a good solution?
Personally, I would choose a different solution.
Thank you for your input. Do you have an alternative solution, or is this the only option for connecting a PT100 sensor onboard?

Here's an example setup: A 1.5 kOhm resistor in series with a PT100 sensor to a 10V input, powered by 24V. PT100 resistance at 0°C = 100Ω, at 100°C ≈ 138Ω. 1500Ω to 100Ω gives 22.50V and 1.50V at 0°C, while 1500Ω to 138Ω gives 22.08V and 1.92V at 100°C. The voltage difference ΔU = 0.42 V over a temperature difference of Δϑ = 100°C. The resolution is about 0.01V = 2.38°C, roughly 2.5°C per step, which is poor. The margin of error is also large for the input range.
This setup reflects the solution I previously described.
If I use a 4-20mA converter with a PT100 and a 500Ω resistor, that results in a 2-10V output. Is it possible to use this range instead of 0-10V DC? Can this be scaled and adjusted as needed?
What temperature range do you want to measure?

Suppose the range is 0 - 80°C. If I input 2V and get a value of 202, can I subtract 202 from the analog input to set the zero point? Is it possible to perform such a mathematical adjustment on the analog input?

Regarding the basics: The A/D converter for an analog input translates 0-10V or 0/4-20mA signals into approximately 1,000 units. If you use a 2-10V (or 4-20mA) input, you only get 800 units, since 200 units for 0-2V (or 0-4mA) are not used. To adjust for this, you need to set the analog amplifier so that a 0-10V (or 4-20mA) signal covers the range, and shift the starting point (OFFSET). For example, 80°C over 800 units results in 0.1°C per unit. At 0.1°C for 1,000 units, you get 100°C. With a measuring range of 80°C, there is an offset of 20°C (200 units). This means the adjusted measurement range stretches from -20°C to 80°C.
I hope this explanation clarifies things. Thank you for your feedback and rating.
